newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France's Chirac, Jospin want EU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France's Chirac, Jospin want EU budget pact.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday he hoped a stability pact limiting the budget deficits of countries that join a single European currency could be concluded on time at a summit in Amsterdam next week.

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, the summit's host, said after talks in Paris with Chirac and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin that the new Socialist-led French government had told him it could accept an agreement without waiting until Jospin presents its policies to parliament on June 19.

Speaking a day after the government requested a delay to study the stability pact, the conservative Chirac said he backed the left-wing administration's drive to get more emphasis on employment in European Union policy.
The French move sparked some anger in Germany, which pressed for the budget discipline accord last December to reassure its public anxious at abandoning the deutschemark to adopt the euro.
After talks with Kok, Chirac said: "France has committed itself to economic and monetary union and is determined that the euro be launched on January 1, 1999.

"That assumes that we examine in Amsterdam the stability and growth pact, which I hope can be concluded in Amsterdam, and also the social measures and economic policy coordination which the French government has rightly just emphasised," he said.

His remarks also appeared aimed at gently forcing Jospin's hand into accepting a deal at the June 16-17 summit in the first genteel tug-of-war of "cohabitation" between a president and government from opposite political parties.
Socialist European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici repeated earlier on Tuesday he did not believe the French review of the pact could be concluded in time for Amsterdam.
But Jospin said after a separate meeting with Kok: "There are efforts to be made. We will make them."

Kok told reporters both French leaders had shown a "firm will" to reach a deal by the weekend, and Jospin had assured him he did not have to wait until presenting his keynote policy statement to parliament on June 19.
Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm would be preparing a series of texts to resolve the dispute, he said.
An official in Chirac's office said the president was determined that France should speak with one voice on Europe.

Both Chirac and Kok said they were optimistic that the summit would also be able to conclude negotiations on reforming European Union institutions, which some analysts had suggested might be put at risk because of the row over the stability pact.
Kok said the new French government had not proposed any changes to the EU reform treaty on the table.

Kok sought to address Jospin's concerns, telling reporters the French government was not alone in wanting to stress jobs. All EU member states sought a Europe which was not just monetarist but also focused on employment, he said.
"It is important to see how one can develop an additional element on top of the stability pact" to promote jobs, he said.
Kok, current holder of the EU's rotating presidency, said he hoped for "good preparations" on the stability pact before Amsterdam, but he added "there is no guarantee."

European Union leaders negotiated the pact -- which would limit euro-zone countries' public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product after 1999 -- at a summit in Dublin last December but they are due to formally approve it next week.

European Commission president Jacques Santer is due in Paris on Thursday for talks aimed at resolving French concerns over the stability pact, and Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will meet German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday.
Kok was also due to meet Kohl on Wednesday.
